norms.heading: Antenuptial (premarital) agreements — validity and enforceability
norms.summary_rule: “In Missouri, to be valid and enforceable a prenuptial agreement must be entered into freely, fairly, knowingly, understandingly, and in good faith with full disclosure.” (Short v. Short, 2011; Potts v. Potts, 2010; Penrod v. Penrod, 2021). “Prenuptial agreements will be upheld and will dispose of issues of property division unless found to be unconscionable.” (O'Connor v. Miroslaw, 2012). “Missouri courts have equally applied these provisions to the terms of an antenuptial agreement by holding that they are binding unless the court finds the agreement unconscionable.” (Riney v. Riney, 2024, referring to the § 452.325 unconscionability standard).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Short v. Short, 356 S.W.3d 235 (Mo. App. E.D. 2011)
Leading source: Potts v. Potts, 303 S.W.3d 177 (Mo. App. W.D. 2010)
Leading source: William J. Penrod v. Karen D. Penrod, No. ED109069 (Mo. App. E.D. 2021)
Leading source: O'Connor v. Miroslaw, 388 S.W.3d 541 (Mo. App. W.D. 2012)
Leading source: Richard P. Riney v. Margaret M. Riney, No. ED111743 (Mo. App. E.D. 2024)

norms.heading: Postnuptial agreements — same test as antenuptial agreements
norms.summary_rule: “In determining whether a postnuptial agreement is valid, we apply the same rules used to determine if an antenuptial agreement is valid.” (In re Marriage of Bell, 2011). Relevant factors include “the waiving spouse’s access to independent counsel and understanding of the agreement, disclosure of the assets and their values, disclosure of the spouse’s legal rights, and the relative equality of the bargaining positions between each spouse” (Bell, summarising J.A.D. v. F.J.D., Mo. banc 1998).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Marriage of Bell v. Bell, 360 S.W.3d 270 (Mo. App. S.D. 2011)

norms.heading: Separation agreements — binding effect and unconscionability review (§ 452.325)
norms.summary_rule: “Generally speaking, the terms of a separation agreement in a proceeding for dissolution of marriage are binding upon the court unless the court finds the separation agreement is unconscionable.” (Tierney v. Tierney, 2025). “An agreement is unconscionable if it involves “an inequality so strong, gross, and manifest that it must be impossible to state it to one with common sense without producing an exclamation at the inequality of it.”” (Landers v. Sgouros, 2007; In re Marriage of Thompson, 2000). The test “is not measured by the factors delineated in § 452.330” (Thompson, quoting In re Marriage of Turner).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Linda J. Tierney v. Lawrence J. Tierney, No. ED112742 (Mo. App. E.D. 2025)
Leading source: In re the Marriage Thompson, 27 S.W.3d 502 (Mo. App. S.D. 2000)
Leading source: Landers v. Sgouros, 224 S.W.3d 651 (Mo. App. S.D. 2007)

norms.heading: Contract interpretation applied to separation / marital settlement agreements incorporated in decrees
norms.summary_rule: “A separation agreement is a contract.” (Boden v. Boden, 2007). “The terms of the separation agreement, incorporated into the 1990 dissolution decree, are construed according to the principles governing contract interpretation.” “The cardinal rule in the interpretation of a contract is to ascertain the intention of the parties and to give effect to that intention.” (Roberts v. Roberts, 2014). Likewise, “marital settlement agreements are construed using ordinary contract principles.” (LeKander v. Estate of LeKander, 2011).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Roberts v. Roberts, 432 S.W.3d 789 (Mo. App. W.D. 2014)
Leading source: Boden v. Boden, 229 S.W.3d 169 (Mo. App. E.D. 2007)
Leading source: Lekander v. Estate of Lekander, 345 S.W.3d 282 (Mo. App. S.D. 2011)

norms.heading: Maintenance under separation agreements — decretal, contractual and non-modifiable maintenance
norms.summary_rule: “Contractual maintenance, on the other hand, arises where the “maintenance provisions were not to be incorporated into the decree.”” “Contractual maintenance is enforceable by a separate action for breach of contract.” Maintenance set forth in the decree but agreed to be non-modifiable is a “hybrid” that “is decretal for purposes of enforcement and contractual for purposes of modification.” (Cates v. Cates, Mo. banc 1991). “In other words, separation agreement decretal maintenance is modifiable, unless the parties specifically agree to preclude or limit modification.” (Lueckenotte v. Lueckenotte, Mo. banc 2001, applying § 452.325.6).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Cates v. Cates, 819 S.W.2d 731 (Mo. banc 1991)
Leading source: Lueckenotte v. Lueckenotte, 34 S.W.3d 387 (Mo. banc 2001)

norms.heading: Presumption of marital property — clear and convincing evidence to rebut
norms.summary_rule: “[a] party who claims that property, presumed to be marital, is in fact separate property assumes the burden of rebutting the presumption with clear and convincing evidence” (James v. James, Mo. banc 2002, applying § 452.330.3).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: James v. James, 108 S.W.3d 1 (Mo. banc 2002)

norms.heading: Source-of-funds rule for classifying property
norms.summary_rule: “But the inception of title theory is losing favor to the “source of funds” rule which is considered to be more equitable.” “Under the source of funds rule, the character of the property is determined by the source of funds financing the purchase.” (Hoffmann v. Hoffmann, Mo. banc 1984). “At trial, the spouse advocating application of the source-of-funds rule to characterize non-marital property as marital property bears the burden of proving that there was an increase in value of the non-marital property due to marital labor or other marital assets.” (Torres v. Torres, 2020).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Hofmann v. Hoffmann, 676 S.W.2d 817 (Mo. banc 1984)
Leading source: Shelbie Torres v. Alejandro Raul Torres, No. WD82498 (Mo. App. W.D. 2020)

norms.heading: Transmutation of separate property into marital property
norms.summary_rule: “Missouri recognizes the concept of transmutation which turns non-marital property into marital property as a consequence of a transfer of that property, either as a gift or by express or implied agreement of the spouses.” (Carter v. Carter, 2025). “[P]lacing separate property into the joint names of both spouses creates a presumption that the property has been transmuted into marital property.” (Eckelkamp v. Eckelkamp, 2020).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Melissa M. Carter v. Drew B. Carter, No. ED112335 (Mo. App. E.D. 2025)
Leading source: Virginia G. Eckelkamp v. Gary L. Eckelkamp, No. ED108437 (Mo. App. E.D. 2020)

norms.heading: Commingling and tracing of separate property
norms.summary_rule: “In addition, section 452.330.4 specifically states that nonmarital property does not become marital property solely because it is commingled with marital property.” “Instead, onee commingling occurs, the party claiming a separate property interest must establish by clear and convincing evidence that an identifiable portion can be traced to specific separate property.” (Andrews v. Andrews, 2009; the reporter text reads “onee” [sic] for “once”). “Once commingling occurs, the party claiming separate property has the burden of establishing that an identifiable portion of the funds can be traced to specific nonmarital assets.” (Keet v. Bell, 2016). “It was husband’s burden to trace the non-marital property into his capital contributions” (Bold v. Bold, Mo. banc 1995).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Andrews v. Andrews, 289 S.W.3d 717 (Mo. App. E.D. 2009)
Leading source: Keet v. Bell, 481 S.W.3d 855 (Mo. App. S.D. 2016)
Leading source: Bold v. Bold, 912 S.W.2d 477 (Mo. banc 1995)

norms.heading: Valuation of marital property
norms.summary_rule: “A trial court enjoys broad discretion in valuing marital property.” (Meier v. Meier, 2010). “A trial court has broad discretion in valuing marital property, but it cannot enter a valuation that is not supported by any evidence.” (Hayes v. Hayes, 2009). “A court values marital property as of the time of trial.” (Kratzer v. Kratzer, 2017); “Marital property is valued as of the date of trial.” (Seggelke v. Seggelke, 2010).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Meier v. Meier, 306 S.W.3d 692 (Mo. App. E.D. 2010)
Leading source: Hayes v. Hayes, 288 S.W.3d 823 (Mo. App. S.D. 2009)
Leading source: Kratzer v. Kratzer, 520 S.W.3d 809 (Mo. App. E.D. 2017)
Leading source: Seggelke v. Seggelke, 319 S.W.3d 461 (Mo. App. E.D. 2010)

norms.heading: Recognition of foreign-country divorce, custody and support judgments — comity
norms.summary_rule: “Based on the doctrine of comity, state and federal courts may give recognition and force and effect to judgments obtained in foreign countries to the same extent as in the case of judgments of sister states.” “A divorce decree obtained in a foreign country or a sister state carries a rebuttable presumption of validity.” (Manor v. Manor, 1991, Israeli support judgment). “In contrast to the full faith and credit clause of the federal constitution, which imposes obligations on the courts of a sister state, the doctrine of comity is a rule of voluntary consent” and “to apply the doctrine, the court must have the law of the foreign country properly before it.” (T.H. v. A.S., 1997). “Comity and the duty to recognize the validity and effect of court proceedings in a foreign jurisdiction are not regarded as absolute rights, but are rather self-imposed restraints.” (Welch v. Contreras, 2005).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Manor v. Manor, 811 S.W.2d 497 (Mo. App. E.D. 1991)
Leading source: T.H. v. A.S., 938 S.W.2d 910 (Mo. App. W.D. 1997)
Leading source: Welch v. Contreras, 174 S.W.3d 53 (Mo. App. W.D. 2005)

norms.heading: Choice of law for marital agreements — Restatement (Second) Conflict of Laws §§ 187–188
norms.summary_rule: Express choice-of-law clauses in antenuptial agreements are given effect (Rivers v. Rivers, 2000, distinguishing cases in which “the respective antenuptial agreements contained express choice of law provisions”); “Section 187(1) of the Restatement gives effect to the parties’ contractual choice of law “if the particular issue is one which the parties could have resolved by an explicit provision in their agreement directed to that issue.”” (Armstrong Business Services v. H & R Block, 2002). “In the absence of an effective choice of law, Missouri uses the criteria found in section 188, The Restatement (Second) of Conflicts of Law (1971), in determining whether Missouri law, or that of a sister state should apply.” “Under the Restatement (Second) Conflicts of Law criteria, Missouri law would apply to the interpretation of the parties’ premarital agreement because Missouri is where performance of the contract is to take place and the parties were residents of Missouri when the dissolution action was filed.” (Rivers). Section 188 “provides that the law of the state with the most significant relationship to the transaction and parties governs.” (Viacom, Inc. v. Transit Casualty Co., Mo. banc 2004).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Rivers v. Rivers, 21 S.W.3d 117 (Mo. App. W.D. 2000)
Leading source: Viacom, Inc. v. Transit Casualty Co., 138 S.W.3d 723 (Mo. banc 2004)
Leading source: Armstrong Business Services, Inc. v. H & R Block, 96 S.W.3d 867 (Mo. App. W.D. 2002)

norms.heading: Personal jurisdiction over nonresident spouses and parents
norms.summary_rule: “Rule 54.06(b) mandates compliance with the minimum contacts test by requiring that one whom the state would subject to an in personam judgment for maintenance, support, attorney’s fees, suit money, or disposition of marital property must have “lived in lawful marriage within this state.”” (Crouch v. Crouch, Mo. banc 1982; followed in Patel v. Patel, 2012, and Wilson v. Wilson, 2023). Due process requires that a nonresident defendant “have certain minimum contacts with it such that the maintenance of the suit does not offend “traditional notions of fair play and substantial justice.”” (Crouch).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Crouch v. Crouch, 641 S.W.2d 86 (Mo. banc 1982)
Leading source: Patel v. Patel, 380 S.W.3d 625 (Mo. App. W.D. 2012)
Leading source: Angela Christine Wilson v. Christopher Darnell Wilson, No. WD85210 (Mo. App. W.D. 2023)

norms.heading: Maintenance: two-step threshold (need) and balancing (ability to pay)
norms.summary_rule: Section 452.335 “provides a two-step process for an award of maintenance.” (Archdekin v. Archdekin, Mo. banc 2018). “As a prerequisite to awarding spousal maintenance, section 452.335 requires the party seeking maintenance to establish he or she "[l]acks sufficient property, including marital property apportioned to him , to provide for his reasonable needs."” (Archdekin). “When a party requests maintenance, the trial court must follow a two-step process to determine if maintenance is warranted.” (Wilkerson, 2025). “If the trial court determines the party seeking maintenance cannot meet their reasonable needs, the trial court must apply the factors of Section 452.335.2” so as to balance the reasonable needs of the spouse seeking maintenance against the ability of the other spouse to pay (McVean, 2025).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Archdekin v. Archdekin, 562 S.W.3d 298 (Mo. banc 2018)
Leading source: CLAIRE S. WILKERSON v. CLAY M. WILKERSON, No. SD38454 (Mo. App. S.D. 2025)
Leading source: Joy Janelle McVean, Respondent, vs. Anthony David McVean, Appellant., No. ED112557 (Mo. App. E.D. 2025)

norms.heading: Relocation of a child: burden on the relocating parent (good faith and best interests)
norms.summary_rule: Section 452.377.9 “drops the requirement that the non-relocating parent show good faith in opposing the move and simply requires the relocating parent to shoulder the burden of establishing good faith in proposing the move.” (Herigon v. Herigon, 2003). Relocation is allowed where the court finds that the “proposed relocation was made in good faith and is in the best interest of the minor child” (Dorman v. Dorman, 2002).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Herigon v. Herigon, 121 S.W.3d 562 (Mo. App. W.D. 2003)
Leading source: Dorman v. Dorman, 91 S.W.3d 167 (Mo. App. W.D. 2002)

norms.heading: Guardian ad litem in custody proceedings — role
norms.summary_rule: “Mandatory appointment of a guardian ad litem is not intended to benefit either of the parties in a dissolution proceeding.” (Rombach v. Rombach, Mo. banc 1993). “Alleged inaction of a guardian ad litem, if any, is not tantamount to a claim of trial court error.” (Mund v. Mund, Mo. banc 1999).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Rombach v. Rombach, 867 S.W.2d 500 (Mo. banc 1993)
Leading source: Mund v. Mund, 7 S.W.3d 401 (Mo. banc 1999)

norms.heading: Civil contempt for non-payment of support or maintenance — purge and appealability
norms.summary_rule: A party held in civil contempt may either “(1) purge himself of the contempt by complying with the [circuit] court’s order, making the case moot and unappealable; or (2) appeal the order, but only after the [circuit] court’s order is enforced by incarceration or otherwise.” (Vaught, 2025, quoting Emmons). Civil contempt is available to enforce support: “Based on these findings, Father was in civil contempt for failure to pay his child support.” (Whitton, 2025).

alt_urls.label:
Leading source: Renee T. Vaught (a/k/a Renee Lepper, a/k/a Renee Wilde)
vs.
Shawn Vaught, No. WD87742 (Mo. App. W.D. 2025)
Leading source: Jon P. Whitton v. Heather A. Whitton (NKA Peterson), No. WD86940 (Mo. App. W.D. 2025)

norms.heading: Emancipation — burden of proof
norms.summary_rule: The party asserting emancipation bears the burden: “Under Wurth plaintiff has the burden of proving that she is emancipated and under the evidence presented at the hearing she cannot sustain that burden.” (Fugate ex rel. Stroup v. Fugate, Mo. banc 1979); applied in Kay v. Keller (2015), where the father argued “Mother failed to meet her burden of proving emancipation.”

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Fugate ex rel. Stroup v. Fugate, 582 S.W.2d 663 (Mo. banc 1979)
Leading source: Kay v. Keller, 462 S.W.3d 748 (Mo. App. W.D. 2015)

norms.heading: Retroactive child support — limits
norms.summary_rule: “The trial court should also determine whether to make the order of child support retroactive to the date of the filing of the motion to modify child support and personal service.” (Lueckenotte v. Lueckenotte, Mo. banc 2001). “Although trial courts have discretion under Section 452.340.1 to award retroactive child support, that discretion extends only to the date the petition for dissolution was filed, and Missouri courts have determined that an award predating that filing constitutes an abuse of discretion.” (Lollar, 2019). Section 452.340.1 “permits but does not require an order of retroactive child support from the date of the filing of the petition.” (Hanson, 2018).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Lueckenotte v. Lueckenotte, 34 S.W.3d 387 (Mo. banc 2001)
Leading source: Christine Ann Lollar v. Richard Dwain Lollar, No. ED106488 (Mo. App. E.D. 2019)
Leading source: Hanson v. Hanson (In re Hanson), 540 S.W.3d 512 (Mo. App. S.D. 2018)

norms.heading: Attorney-fee awards in family cases (§ 452.355)
norms.summary_rule: “Section 452.355 authorizes the circuit court to award attorney fees while taking into consideration “all relevant factors including the financial resources of both parties, the merits of the case and the actions of the parties during the pendency of the action....” (Goins v. Goins, Mo. banc 2013); “the court is authorized to award attorney fees “after considering all relevant factors including the financial resources of both parties ....” (Kohring v. Snodgrass, Mo. banc 1999).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Goins v. Goins, 406 S.W.3d 886 (Mo. banc 2013)
Leading source: Kohring v. Snodgrass, 999 S.W.2d 228 (Mo. banc 1999)

norms.heading: Grandparent visitation — constitutional limits (Troxel)
norms.summary_rule: Parents argued that if the statute as construed in Herndon v. Tuhey “permits a court to interfere with a fit parent’s decision not to allow a child to visit with the child’s grandparents, the statute violates their constitutional right to raise their children free from unnecessary state interference as recognized in Troxel” (Blakely v. Blakely, Mo. banc 2002). “Earlier cases also support this interpretation because the provision requiring an unreasonable denial of visitation for more than 90 days prevents the Missouri grandparent-visitation statute from being held unconstitutional.” (Massman v. Massman, 2016).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Blakely v. Blakely, 83 S.W.3d 537 (Mo. banc 2002)
Leading source: Massman v. Massman, 505 S.W.3d 406 (Mo. App. E.D. 2016)

norms.heading: Ability to pay child support — earning capacity and resources
norms.summary_rule: “In determining a parent’s ability to pay child support, a court may consider past, present, and anticipated earning capacity.” (Carter, 2025). “While a party’s salary is usually the most significant component of a parent’s ability to pay child support, the court may consider other resources” (Selleck v. Selleck, 2017). “Instead, in determining ability to pay, the focus is on whether the individual after making required child support payments can meet his remaining needs and obligations.” (Kropf v. Jones, 2015).

alt_urls.label: Leading source: Melissa M. Carter v. Drew B. Carter, No. ED112335 (Mo. App. E.D. 2025)
Leading source: Selleck v. Selleck, 528 S.W.3d 471 (Mo. App. E.D. 2017)
Leading source: Kropf v. Jones, 489 S.W.3d 830 (Mo. App. E.D. 2015)
